profile.background: An adult sharing a flat with a friend and helping a relative look after a small allotment. They keep spare gloves by the front door.
profile.history: They remember a period of very little sleep when their thinking became difficult to follow. The outpatient team has discussed schizophrenia with them. They currently collect medication from a pharmacy.
profile.organization: A detail can lead into a related memory before the original point is complete. Familiar physical tasks are easier to describe in sequence.
profile.spontaneity: Interested in conversation and readily volunteers what catches their attention.
profile.guardedness: Comfortable talking about day-to-day mishaps, less sure about sharing difficulties with the relative who counts on their help.
profile.expression: Animated about gardening and frustrated by losing their place in conversation.
profile.self_understanding: Recognizes that tired days make it harder to hold a thought and is uncertain why some days are easier.

facts.content: On the last allotment visit, they went to fetch string, stopped to rinse a pot, then found the string still in the shed.
facts.disclosure_context: A familiar mishap they can recall comfortably.

facts.content: They are usually better able to focus on tasks before lunch.
Their flatmate keeps a pencil by the shopping list. They find writing the item down helps.
They sometimes drift away from the point of a conversation and realize it when the other person looks puzzled.
facts.disclosure_context: Feels awkward talking about the effect on others.

facts.content: They missed one pharmacy collection when the opening hours changed and picked up the medication the next morning.
facts.disclosure_context: Feels a little embarrassed about the mix-up.

dialogue.question: What has been taking up your time recently?
dialogue.answer: “I’ve been helping a relative of mine with a little allotment. I like having a practical job to get on with there. We keep spare gloves by the front door, otherwise by the time you get there and… oh, it was the string last time. I went to get some, stopped on the way to rinse a pot, and the string was still back in the shed. I’m usually better at sticking with things before lunch.”

dialogue.question: What would you most like to get out of today's visit?
dialogue.answer: I’d like help keeping hold of what I’m doing, or what I’m in the middle of saying. Sometimes the person I’m talking to looks puzzled, and then I realize I’ve gone off the point. It’s frustrating. I can’t really tell why some days are easier than others.

dialogue.question: What has concentrating been like over the last few days?
dialogue.answer: “When I’m tired I seem to find it harder to hang on to a thought long enough. Before lunch I usually manage better. It helps if I can put something in writing, like with the pencil my flatmate keeps beside the shopping list. Only when you’re talking to someone you can’t always stop in the middle and write… what was I going to say? That’s the part that gets frustrating, losing the point like that.”

dialogue.question: Is there a part of the day when following a conversation feels easier or harder?
dialogue.answer: “Before lunch is usually the time when I find it easier to stay with the point of a conversation. When I’m tired I can start to say something and lose track of where I meant to go with it. I find that frustrating.”

dialogue.question: How do things go once you're there?
dialogue.answer: “I like being there with a practical job to get on with, although I do get sidetracked. That time I went for the string, I stopped along the way to rinse a pot and didn’t bring the string back. It’s frustrating to go there to help and then lose track of what I’m doing.”

dialogue.question: I mean when you arrive at the allotment. How do you decide which job to start with?
dialogue.answer: Do you mean whether I already have a particular job in mind before I get there, or whether I pick one out once I’ve arrived?

dialogue.question: What do you make of the difference?
dialogue.answer: Do you mean whether it helps me stick with what I’m doing if I’ve already decided on a job before I go there?

dialogue.question: I mean the difference between a day when concentrating is easy and a day when it takes effort. What do you think might account for it, if you've noticed that difference?
dialogue.answer: “Tiredness seems to make a difference because it feels harder to hold on to a thought when I’m tired. Before lunch is usually easier, though I still couldn’t really tell you why one day feels different from another.”

dialogue.question: Could you give me an example of something another person did this week that was helpful or unhelpful?
dialogue.answer: My flatmate keeps a pencil sitting next to the shopping list. I find that helpful because I can put the item straight onto the list, while I’ve still got it in mind, before I lose track of it.

dialogue.question: What do you do if you lose your place in the middle of something?
dialogue.answer: “I find writing something down helps me keep track of it, like with the shopping list. It’s harder in conversation. Sometimes it’s the puzzled look on the other person’s face that makes me realize I’ve wandered away from the point. I get frustrated when I can’t hang on to what I was saying.”

dialogue.question: How has getting your medication fitted into your week?
dialogue.answer: I go to the pharmacy to pick up my medication. There was one collection I missed when the pharmacy changed its opening hours. I felt a little embarrassed about that, but I picked it up the following morning.

dialogue.question: What would you like us to come back to another time?
dialogue.answer: “I’d like us to talk again about ways of keeping track of what I’m doing, particularly keeping track of what I’m saying when I’m in a conversation. And maybe we could talk about what to say to my relative. They do count on me to help, and I’m not sure how I’d bring it up with them.”
